title: Honjo Mudguards in Tokyo, Japan: Juxtaposition – John Watson
content:
Continuing our third and final Reportage from the legacy makers of Japan, today we share the workshop of Tokyo’s Honjo Mudguards. Read on for a collaboration between The Radavist and Slow Spin Society…

Set and Setting

We landed at our business hotel in Eastern Tokyo after a quick stop at Berth Coffee for a light-roasted pour-over, feeling lightly roasted myself. Cari had never spent the night in a business hotel, but during my eight trips to Japan in the early aughts, I found them to be the cheapest options without sacrificing creature comforts to the level of a hostel.

I drop my backpack on the floor and remove the padded camera case, open my laptop, and start to dump images. Rarely do I review photos on camera while on site for shoots like this; it’s like getting scans back from a roll of film, so I flip through each image and study it. Shooting this entire Shop Visit series with a manual focus rangefinder with a f1.4 lens bayonet has been interesting, to say the least, but I’m overwhelmingly pleased with the photos, noting only one or two missed focus shots.

Landing focus on a razor’s edge, finding the iris of one’s eye, or the edge of a piece of millimeter-thick metal has been an exercise in patience, but I knew the result from this labor would be the absolute best imagery I could muster.

Gear Oil

“My hair smells like gear oil,” Cari says as she’s figuring out the shower situation. We have dinner with Masashi in an hour, so as the photos populate my Lightroom, we’re getting ready. I sniff my favorite camo jacket. Yep. The acridity is all-too present on its fibers. Reaching for the bottle of fabric freshener hanging in the closet, I give it a dose.

As we’re leaving for dinner, my upload is complete, and I sigh with relief. The third Shop Visit in as many days, and I was pleased.

After dinner, I scroll through, culling the 600 images down to 200 and then down to the gallery you see here. Export. Backup. Close the laptop and go to bed.

It’s now been a week, and I’m returning to these images to write about my experience at Honjo Fenders. Inside this cramped, dimly-lit space, it’s stuffed to the brim with heavy-duty machinery, empty buckets of gear fluid, and stacks of protective film-wrapped fenders, so elegantly arranged they look like the scales of an ancient dragon.

All in the “Honjo” neighborhood of the eastern Sumida Ward, Tokyo, perched at the base of the Skytree tower.

Honjo Legacy

Established in 1949 by Matashiro Shimamura, Honjo Mudguards makes the most beautiful fenders from an approximately ~2000 sqft workshop over two levels. After Matashiro, his son, Yukio Shimamura, took the wheel of the operation, and now Tomoyuki Shimamura, aka Tomo-san, runs the show with a handful of other employees.

The machines within the space range from the 1940s through the 1970s, including a giant hydraulic press used by the company to make motorcycle fenders, which are about 5% of the company’s current market share. The other 95% is all bicycle fenders and bells. Due to the simplicity and scale of this workshop, Honjo operates on a per-order fulfillment system. If a company like Sim Works orders 100 fenders, the team will work from start to finish, knocking out the punch list of fender types.

Fender Process

Raw material arrives in 1 km-long rolls of varying widths, with each roll making approximately 500 pairs of fenders. There are eight different widths of rolls. Honjo primarily works with aluminum but also utilizes brass and stainless steel. In the back, along the main party wall of the shop, there’s a shelf of dozens of fender profile dies, each labeled by width and profile.

Similar to MKS’ process and how viewing the procedure creates a visceral sense of value, Honjo’s fender production is an art form in itself. The material enters a die press conveyor belt, with 7 various dies that form the fender lips before it dispenses in a coil at the end. This coil of formed fenders is then cut, depending on the wheel diameter. There are two machines that are used in this manner; one is individually fed pre-cut pieces, and the other is roll-fed.

From there, the fenders take on a journey, receiving either fluting by that massive press, or final radiusing if they’re the flatter profiles. The flat fenders are vastly faster to make; it’s the fluted and hammered profiles that take from 40 minutes to an hour of intense hand and machine forming that are the most labor-intensive.

If the fender requires hammer-finishing, that process is IP, and Tomo-san said with a smile that it’s a family secret.

Once the fender’s form is finalized – be it flutes or flat – it goes through a radius machine, where each fender is fed through a series of dies that give the fender its diameter depending on wheel size. It takes four to five passes to nail the correct shape, and with each pass, the fender is checked with a radius piece of steel.

Each fender is stacked on sheets of cardboard on top of each run. The cardboard-lined fender piles are then loaded into a freight elevator and taken upstairs for final finishing. There, an employee will trim them, hand-polish each, and add the Honjo label before being placed in a plastic sleeve for shipping.

Sim Works Turtle Bells

In 2019, Sim Works finally launched its collaboration with Honjo: the Turtle Bell. It took three years to develop the product and was the first product outside of a new fender profile that Honjo had taken on since its founding. What’s mind-numbing about the forming of the bells is that while Honjo has a 55-ton press, the forming of the bells requires 75 tons of pressure, requiring the brand to outsource the brass forming to a local shop close by.

Crates of bells arrive from the outsourced shop and from there, they undergo an intense die process to add the texturing. Tomo-san disappears for a few minutes while retrieving the dies aboard a heavy-duty cart. The bell body undergoes three passes, where the recessed hexagon pattern is pressed into the bell shape. They’re then assembled by hand.

This process takes 40 minutes per bell, and at its current capacity, Honjo can only produce 200 bells a year, which requires a 6-month lead time. Sim Works is constantly selling out of these bells and is on a permanent purchase order with Honjo. So if you see these bells in stock at Sim Works, act quickly!

The Radavist x Slow Spin Society

As The Radavist celebrates its 20th anniversary of covering cycling communities, we wanted to partner with the next generation of cycling media on a lifelong dream trip of mine. We’ve featured Paul from Slow Spin Society on the website before. As a wearer of many hats – Paul also works for Sim Works as its Euro branch and was gracious enough to act as our Japanese translator during the trip – Paul is always balancing his job at Sim Works with Slow Spin. As we chatted about what a possible collaboration could look like, we landed on the idea of storytelling and interviews.

Paul did a deep dive interview with Tomo-san, so roll on over to Slow Spin Society to read Paul’s Honjo interview!

Handmade in Japan

Every ounce of metal that arrives when you order a pair of fenders is made from raw material in the Honjo factory. Each bracket is stamped, then formed; each piece of bent stay is cut and shaped. Everything is done by hand, from start to finish, by a team of ~four people in a cramped shop in Tokyo, doing it the same way since its opening in 1949.

After this series of Shop Visits to Japanese makers, I kept mulling over a stark dichotomy. These are industrial spaces, with loud, heavy machines, as old as the factories themselves, pressing metal through tons of hydraulic power. Each surface is covered with a thin film of gear oil and what one can only describe as decades of patina.

Yet from these oppressively intimidating beasts come products as elegant as flower petals, designed to withstand a lifetime’s worth of use, fully repairable, with replacement parts readily available, and handmade by three generations of craftsmen and women.

A juxtaposition of 50 years of patina with the shiniest, highest-quality bicycle parts in the world.

Tomo-san and his father Yukio

Philosophies of Craft

There is a Western definition of legacy, which has been lost to globalization, but the Eastern philosophy of the truly handmade legacy, of Mingei 民芸 and Ikigai 生き甲斐, is still very much on display in shops like Honjo. Tomo-san and his family live in a small apartment on the third floor of Honjo, close enough to never escape the smell of cutting fluid or the thuds of machinery, but for them, it is their family’s legacy.

I’ll never look at a pair of Honjo fenders and think they’re too expensive; rather, I’ll consider which bike is worthy of having them installed.

I wanted to extend a warm thank you to the Shimamura family and to Sim Works for making these Shop Visits to Japanese makers a possibility. Thank you to Tomo-san for sharing your process and your life’s work and family’s legacy with us.

And thank you to the people of Japan who have made this trip the most memorable in my life.

Arigato gozaimasu.

The Radavist thanks Sim Works for supporting our independent Reportage here!
